L801@P30: 3.2.7 Concept
L802@P30: The seventh entity defined in the model is concept: an abstract notion or idea.
L803@P30: The entity defined as concept encompasses a comprehensive range of abstractions that
L804@P30: may be the subject of a work: fields of knowledge, disciplines, schools of thought
L805@P30: (philosophies, religions, political ideologies, etc.), theories, processes, techniques,
L806@P30: practices, etc. A concept may be broad in nature or narrowly defined and precise.

L811@P31: □ c4 Supply-side economics
L812@P31: □ ….
L813@P31: For the purposes of this study concepts are treated as entities only to the extent that they
L814@P31: are the subject of a work (e.g., as the subject of a philosophical treatise, of a critique of a
L815@P31: school of thought, etc.). Defining the entity concept enables us to name and identify the

L821@P31: 3.2.8 Object
L822@P31: The eighth entity defined in the model is object: a material thing.
L823@P31: The entity defined as object encompasses a comprehensive range of material things that
L824@P31: may be the subject of a work: animate and inanimate objects occurring in nature; fixed,
L825@P31: movable, and moving objects that are the product of human creation; objects that no
L826@P31: longer exist.

L828@P31: □ o1 Buckingham Palace

L832@P31: □ ….
L833@P31: For the purposes of this study objects are treated as entities only to the extent that they
L834@P31: are the subject of a work (e.g., as the subject of a scientific study, etc.).

L836@P32: manner, independently of the presence, absence, or form of the name for that object that

L840@P32: 3.2.9 Event
L841@P32: The ninth entity defined in the model is event: an action or occurrence.
L842@P32: The entity defined as event encompasses a comprehensive range of actions and
L843@P32: occurrences that may be the subject of a work: historical events, epochs, periods of time,
L844@P32: etc.

L846@P32: □ e1 The Garment Workers’ Strike
L847@P32: □ e2 The Battle of Hastings
L848@P32: □ e3 The Age of Enlightenment

L850@P32: □ ….
L851@P32: For the purposes of this study events are treated as entities only to the extent that they are
L852@P32: the subject of a work (e.g., the subject of an historical treatise, of a painting, etc.).
L853@P32: Defining the entity event enables us to name and identify the event in a consistent
L854@P32: manner, independently of the presence, absence, or form of the name for that event that
L855@P32: appears on or in any particular expression or manifestation of a work.
L856@P32: Defining event as an entity also enables us to draw a relationship between a work and the
L857@P32: event that is the subject of the work.
L858@P32: 3.2.10 Place
L859@P32: The tenth entity defined in the model is place: a location.
L860@P32: The entity defined as place encompasses a comprehensive range of locations: terrestrial
L861@P32: and extra-terrestrial; historical and contemporary; geographic features and geo-political
L862@P32: jurisdictions.

L865@P33: □ pl2 The Alacran Reef

L868@P33: □ ….

L558@P23: realizes is often the most efficient means of grouping related expressions. In effect, the
L559@P23: name we give to the work serves as the name for the entire set or group of expressions
L560@P23: that are realizations of the same intellectual or artistic creation (e.g., Lancelot du Lac). It
L561@P23: is the entity defined as work, therefore, that provides us with this grouping capability.
L562@P23: 3.2.2 Expression
L563@P23: The second entity defined in the model is expression: the intellectual or artistic
L564@P23: realization of a work in the form of alpha-numeric, musical, or choreographic notation,
L565@P23: sound, image, object, movement, etc., or any combination of such forms.
L566@P23: An expression is the specific intellectual or artistic form that a work takes each time it is
L567@P23: “realized.” Expression encompasses, for example, the specific words, sentences,
L568@P23: paragraphs, etc. that result from the realization of a work in the form of a text, or the
L569@P23: particular sounds, phrasing, etc. resulting from the realization of a musical work. The
L570@P23: boundaries of the entity expression are defined, however, so as to exclude aspects of
L571@P23: physical form, such as typeface and page layout, that are not integral to the intellectual or
L572@P23: artistic realization of the work as such. When an expression is accompanied by
L573@P23-24: 19 augmentations, such as illustrations, notes, glosses, etc. that are not integral to the
L574@P24: intellectual or artistic realization of the work, such augmentations are considered to be
L575@P24: separate expressions of their own separate work(s). Such augmentations may, or may
L576@P24: not, be considered significant enough to warrant distinct bibliographic identification.
L577@P24: Inasmuch as the form of expression is an inherent characteristic of the expression, any
L578@P24: change in form (e.g., from alpha-numeric notation to spoken word) results in a new

L605@P24: Defining expression as an entity also enables us to draw relationships between specific
L606@P24: expressions of a work. We can use the entity called expression to identify, for example,
L607@P24: the specific text on which a translation is based, or the specific score used for the
L608@P24: performance of a musical composition.

L1285@P46: The place of publication/distribution of the manifestation is the city, town, or other
L1286@P46: locality associated in the manifestation with the name of the publisher/distributor. The
L1287@P46: place of publication may comprise the name of the state, province, territory, and/or
L1288@P46: country as well as the local place name. A manifestation may be associated with one or

L1290@P46: 4.4.5 Publisher/Distributor
L1291@P46: The publisher/distributor of the manifestation is the individual, group, or organization
L1292@P46: named in the manifestation as being responsible for the publication, distribution, issuing,
L1293@P46: or release of the manifestation. A manifestation may be associated with one or more
L1294@P46: publishers or distributors.
L1295@P46: 4.4.6 Date of Publication/Distribution
L1296@P46: The date of publication/distribution of the manifestation is the date (normally a year) of
L1297@P46: public release of the manifestation. The date may be a single date of publication or
L1298@P46: release, or a range of dates (e.g., in the case of a serial publication).
L1299@P46: In the absence of a date designated as the date of publication or release, a copyright date
L1300@P46: or a date of printing or manufacture may serve as a substitute.
L1301@P46: 4.4.7 Fabricator/Manufacturer
L1302@P46: The fabricator/manufacturer of the manifestation is the individual, group, or organization
L1303@P46: named in the manifestation as being responsible for the fabrication or manufacture of the
L1304@P46: manifestation. A manifestation may be associated with one or more fabricators or
L1305@P46: manufacturers.
L1306@P46: 4.4.8 Series Statement
L1307@P46: A series statement is the word, phrase, or group of characters appearing in the
L1308@P46: manifestation naming the series to which the manifestation belongs. A series statement
L1309@P46: may also include a number designating the sequential position of the manifestation within
L1310@P46: the series. There may be one or more series and/or subseries named in the manifestation.
L1311@P46-47: 42 4.4.9 Form of Carrier
L1312@P47: The form of carrier is the specific class of material to which the physical carrier of the
L1313@P47: manifestation belongs (e.g., sound cassette, videodisc, microfilm cartridge, transparency,
L1314@P47: etc.). The carrier for a manifestation comprising multiple physical components may
L1315@P47: include more than one form (e.g., a filmstrip with an accompanying booklet, a separate
L1316@P47: sound disc carrying the sound track for a film, etc.).
L1317@P47: 4.4.10 Extent of the Carrier
L1318@P47: The extent of the carrier is a quantification of the number of physical units making up the
L1319@P47: carrier (e.g., number of sheets, discs, reels, etc.).
L1320@P47: 4.4.11 Physical Medium
L1321@P47: Physical medium is the type of material from which the carrier is produced (e.g., paper,
L1322@P47: wood, plastic, metal, etc.). The physical medium may include in addition to the base
L1323@P47: material any material that is applied to the base (e.g., oil paint applied to canvas, a
L1324@P47: chemical emulsion applied to a film base, etc.). Each component of a manifestation
L1325@P47: comprising multiple physical components may be produced from a different type of
L1326@P47: material.
L1327@P47: 4.4.12 Capture mode
L1328@P47: Capture mode is the means used to record notation, sound, or images in the production of
L1329@P47: a manifestation (e.g., analogue, acoustic, electric, digital, optical etc.).
L1330@P47: 4.4.13 Dimensions of the Carrier
L1331@P47: The dimensions of the carrier are the measurements of the physical components and/or
L1332@P47: the container of the manifestation. The dimensions may comprise measurements of
L1333@P47: height (e.g., 18 cm bound volume), width (e.g., 8mm film), height x width (e.g., 5 x 5 cm
L1334@P47: slide), height x width x depth (e.g., 9 x 30 x 20 cm model), or diameter (e.g., 30 cm disc).
L1335@P47: 4.4.14 Manifestation Identifier
L1336@P47: The manifestation identifier is a number or code uniquely associated with the
L1348@P48: The source for acquisition or access authorization of a manifestation is the name of a
L1349@P48: publisher, distributor, etc. indicated in the manifestation as the source from which the
L1350@P48: manifestation may be acquired or through whom access may be authorized. The source
L1351@P48: for acquisition/access authorization will normally also include an address for the
L1352@P48: publisher, distributor, etc. A manifestation may be associated with one or more sources.
L1353@P48: 4.4.16 Terms of Availability
L1360@P48: restrictions may be based in copyright, or they may extend beyond the protections
L1361@P48: guaranteed in law to the owner of the copyright.
L1362@P48: 4.4.18 Typeface (Printed Book)
L1363@P48: Typeface is the style of type used to print a book (e.g., Baskerville, Times New Roman,
L1364@P48: etc.)
L1365@P48: 4.4.19 Type Size (Printed Book)
L1366@P48: Type size is the size of the characters in a printed book (e.g., 10 point).
L1367@P48: 4.4.20 Foliation (Hand-Printed Book)
L1368@P48: The foliation of a hand-printed book reflects the number of folds made in a printed sheet
L1369@P48: to form a gathering of leaves (e.g., a sheet folded twice to form a quarto, three times to
L1370@P48: form an octavo, etc.)
L1371@P48-49: 44 4.4.21 Collation (Hand-Printed Book)
L1372@P49: Collation reflects the sequence of gatherings in a book as indicated by signatures on each
L1373@P49: gathering (e.g., four gatherings bearing signatures A through D).
L1374@P49: 4.4.22 Publication Status (Serial)
L1375@P49: Publication status for a manifestation issued as a serial is the status of the serial with
L1376@P49: respect to its continuing publication (i.e., whether it is currently published or has ceased
L1377@P49: publication).
L1378@P49: 4.4.23 Numbering (Serial)
L1379@P49: Numbering for a manifestation issued as a serial is the designation of volume/issue, etc.
L1380@P49: and/or date appearing in the manifestation. The numbering may comprise a numeric,
L1381@P49: alphabetic and/or a date component (e.g., Volume 1, number 1 (January 1971)).
L1382@P49: 4.4.24 Playing Speed (Sound Recording)
L1383@P49: Playing speed for a sound recording is the speed at which the carrier must be operated to
L1384@P49: produce the sound intended (e.g., 33 1/3 rpm, 19 cm/s, etc.)
L1385@P49: 4.4.25 Groove Width (Sound Recording)
L1386@P49: Groove width is indicative of the number of grooves per inch cut on a disc or cylinder
L1387@P49: (e.g., microgroove--i.e., 200 grooves per inch).
L1388@P49: 4.4.26 Kind of Cutting (Sound Recording)
L1389@P49: Kind of cutting is the direction in which the grooves are cut on a disc or cylinder (e.g.,
L1390@P49: lateral, vertical, etc.).
L1391@P49: 4.4.27 Tape Configuration (Sound Recording)
L1392@P49: Tape configuration is the number of tracks on a sound tape (e.g., eight track, twelve
L1393@P49: track).
L1394@P49: 4.4.28 Kind of Sound (Sound Recording)
L1395@P49: The kind of sound reflects the number of sound channels used to make the recording
L1396@P49: (monaural, stereophonic, quadraphonic, etc.).
L1397@P49-50: 45 4.4.29 Special Reproduction Characteristic (Sound Recording)
L1398@P50: A special reproduction characteristic is the equalization system, noise reduction system,
L1399@P50: etc. used in making the recording (e.g., NAB, DBX, Dolby, etc.).
L1400@P50: 4.4.30 Colour (Image)
L1401@P50: Colour is the colour(s), tone(s), etc. (including black and white) used in the production of
L1402@P50: an image.
L1403@P50: 4.4.31 Reduction Ratio (Microform)
L1404@P50: Reduction ratio is the degree to which a text or image has been reduced in the process of
L1405@P50: microfilming (e.g., 42x, etc.). Reduction ratio may also be indicated as a range (e.g., very
L1406@P50: high reduction indicates a reduction in the range of 61x to 90x).

L443@P17: Chapter 5 (sections 5.2.1 through 5.2.3) provides a more detailed explanation of the
L444@P17: relationships between the different types of entities that are depicted in the entityrelationship diagrams in sections 3.1.1. through 3.1.3.
L445@P17: 3.1.1 Group 1 Entities: Work, Expression, Manifestation, Item
L446@P17: The entities in the first group (as depicted in Figure 3.1) represent the different aspects of
L447@P17: user interests in the products of intellectual or artistic endeavour. The entities defined as
L448@P17: work (a distinct intellectual or artistic creation) and expression (the intellectual or artistic
L449@P17: realization of a work) reflect intellectual or artistic content. The entities defined as
L450@P17: manifestation (the physical embodiment of an expression of a work) and item (a single
L451@P17: exemplar of a manifestation), on the other hand, reflect physical form.
L452@P17: The relationships depicted in the diagram indicate that a work may be realized through
L453@P17: one or more than one expression (hence the double arrow on the line that links work to
L454@P17: expression). An expression, on the other hand, is the realization of one and only one work
L455@P17: (hence the single arrow on the reverse direction of that line linking expression to work).
L456@P17: An expression may be embodied in one or more than one manifestation; likewise a
L457@P17: manifestation may embody one or more than one expression. A manifestation, in turn,
L458@P17-18: 13 may be exemplified by one or more than one item; but an item may exemplify one and
L459@P18: only one manifestation.
L460@P18: 3.1.2 Group 2 Entities: Person, Corporate Body
L461@P18: The entities in the second group (outlined in bold in Figure 3.2) represent those
L462@P18: responsible for the intellectual or artistic content, the physical production and
L463@P18: dissemination, or the custodianship of the entities in the first group. The entities in the
L464@P18: second group include person (an individual) and corporate body (an organization or
L465@P18: group of individuals and/or organizations).
L466@P18: The diagram depicts the type of “responsibility” relationships that exist between entities
L467@P18: in the second group and the entities in the first group. The diagram indicates that a work
L468@P18: may be created by one or more than one person and/or one or more than one corporate
L469@P18: body. Conversely, a person or a corporate body may create one or more than one work.
L470@P18: An expression may be realized by one or more than one person and/or corporate body;
L471@P18: and a person or corporate body may realize one or more than one expression. A
L472@P18: manifestation may be produced by one or more than one person or corporate body; a
L473@P18: person or corporate body may produce one or more than one manifestation. An item may
L474@P18: be owned by one or more than one person and/or corporate body; a person or corporate
L475@P18: body may own one or more than one item.
L476@P18-21: 14 15 16 3.1.3 Group 3 Entities: Concept, Object, Event, Place
L477@P21: The entities in the third group (outlined in bold in Figure 3.3) represent an additional set
L478@P21: of entities that serve as the subjects of works. The group includes concept (an abstract
L479@P21: notion or idea), object (a material thing), event (an action or occurrence), and place (a
L480@P21: location).
L481@P21: The diagram depicts the “subject” relationships between entities in the third group and
L482@P21: the work entity in the first group. The diagram indicates that a work may have as its
L483@P21: subject one or more than one concept, object, event, and/or place. Conversely, a concept,
L484@P21: object, event, and/or place may be the subject of one or more than one work.
L485@P21: The diagram also depicts the “subject” relationships between work and the entities in the
L486@P21: first and second groups. The diagram indicates that a work may have as its subject one or
L487@P21: more than one work, expression, manifestation, item, person, and/or corporate body.
L488@P21: 3.2 The Entities
L489@P21: 3.2.1 Work
L490@P21: The first entity defined in the model is work: a distinct intellectual or artistic creation.
L491@P21: A work is an abstract entity; there is no single material object one can point to as the
L492@P21: work. We recognize the work through individual realizations or expressions of the work,
L493@P21: but the work itself exists only in the commonality of content between and among the
L494@P21: various expressions of the work. When we speak of Homer’s Iliad as a work, our point of
L495@P21: reference is not a particular recitation or text of the work, but the intellectual creation that
L496@P21: lies behind all the various expressions of the work.
L497@P21: Because the notion of a work is abstract, it is difficult to define precise boundaries for the
L498@P21: entity. The concept of what constitutes a work and where the line of demarcation lies
L499@P21: between one work and another may in fact be viewed differently from one culture to
L500@P21: another. Consequently the bibliographic conventions established by various cultures or
L501@P21: national groups may differ in terms of the criteria they use for determining the boundaries
L502@P21: between one work and another.
L503@P21: For the purposes of this study variant texts incorporating revisions or updates to an earlier
L504@P21: text are viewed simply as expressions of the same work (i.e., the variant texts are not
L505@P21: viewed as separate works). Similarly, abridgements or enlargements of an existing text,
L506@P21: or the addition of parts or an accompaniment to a musical composition are considered to
L507@P21: be different expressions of the same work. Translations from one language to another,
L508@P21-22: 17 musical transcriptions and arrangements, and dubbed or subtitled versions of a film are
L509@P22: also considered simply as different expressions of the same original work.
L510@P22: Examples
L511@P22: □ w1 Henry Gray’s Anatomy of the human body
L512@P22: □ e1 text and illustrations for the first edition
L513@P22: □ e2 text and illustrations for the second edition
L514@P22: □ e3 text and illustrations for the third edition
L515@P22: □ ….
L516@P22: □ w1 J. S. Bach’s The art of the fugue
L517@P22: □ e1 the composer’s score for organ
L518@P22: □ e2 an arrangement for chamber orchestra by Anthony Lewis
L519@P22: □ ….
L520@P22: □ w1 Jules et Jim (motion picture)
L521@P22: □ e1 the original French language version
L522@P22: □ e2 the original with English subtitles added
L523@P22: □ ….
L524@P22: By contrast, when the modification of a work involves a significant degree of
L525@P22: independent intellectual or artistic effort, the result is viewed, for the purpose of this
L526@P22: study, as a new work. Thus paraphrases, rewritings, adaptations for children, parodies,
L527@P22: musical variations on a theme and free transcriptions of a musical composition are
L528@P22: considered to represent new works. Similarly, adaptations of a work from one literary or
L529@P22: art form to another (e.g., dramatizations, adaptations from one medium of the graphic arts
L530@P22: to another, etc.) are considered to represent new works. Abstracts, digests and summaries
L531@P22: are also considered to represent new works.

L540@P23: On a pragmatic level, defining work as an entity in the model serves a number of
L541@P23: purposes. It enables us to give a name and draw relationships to the abstract intellectual
L542@P23: or artistic creation that encompasses all the individual expressions of that work. Thus,
L543@P23: when we describe a work of literary criticism dealing with Homer’s Iliad, for example,
L544@P23: we are able to relate the work of criticism to the work that it treats as its subject. By
L545@P23: naming Homer’s work and defining the relationship between it and the work of criticism,
L546@P23: we are able to indicate that the subject of the work of criticism is in fact the abstraction
L547@P23: we know as the Iliad, and not any specific expression of that work.
L548@P23: Defining work as an entity also enables us to establish indirect relationships between
L549@P23: expressions of the same work in cases where we are unable to draw direct relationships
L550@P23: between individual expressions. For example, there may exist many translations of a
L551@P23: work (e.g., Anne of Green Gables), and it may not always be possible or necessary to
L552@P23: specify the text that has served as the basis for a given translation. In that case we do not
L553@P23: draw a direct relationship between individual expressions of the work (i.e., between the
L554@P23: translation and the text or texts on which the translation was based), but we relate those
L555@P23: and other texts and translations of the work implicitly by relating each of them to the
L556@P23: entity we call the work.
L557@P23: Relating expressions of a work indirectly by relating each expression to the work that it
L558@P23: realizes is often the most efficient means of grouping related expressions. In effect, the
L559@P23: name we give to the work serves as the name for the entire set or group of expressions
L560@P23: that are realizations of the same intellectual or artistic creation (e.g., Lancelot du Lac). It
L561@P23: is the entity defined as work, therefore, that provides us with this grouping capability.
L562@P23: 3.2.2 Expression
L563@P23: The second entity defined in the model is expression: the intellectual or artistic
L564@P23: realization of a work in the form of alpha-numeric, musical, or choreographic notation,
L565@P23: sound, image, object, movement, etc., or any combination of such forms.
L566@P23: An expression is the specific intellectual or artistic form that a work takes each time it is
L567@P23: “realized.” Expression encompasses, for example, the specific words, sentences,
L568@P23: paragraphs, etc. that result from the realization of a work in the form of a text, or the
L569@P23: particular sounds, phrasing, etc. resulting from the realization of a musical work. The
L570@P23: boundaries of the entity expression are defined, however, so as to exclude aspects of
L571@P23: physical form, such as typeface and page layout, that are not integral to the intellectual or
L572@P23: artistic realization of the work as such. When an expression is accompanied by
L573@P23-24: 19 augmentations, such as illustrations, notes, glosses, etc. that are not integral to the
L574@P24: intellectual or artistic realization of the work, such augmentations are considered to be
L575@P24: separate expressions of their own separate work(s). Such augmentations may, or may
L576@P24: not, be considered significant enough to warrant distinct bibliographic identification.
L577@P24: Inasmuch as the form of expression is an inherent characteristic of the expression, any
L578@P24: change in form (e.g., from alpha-numeric notation to spoken word) results in a new
L579@P24: expression. Similarly, changes in the intellectual conventions or instruments that are
L580@P24: employed to express a work (e.g., translation from one language to another) result in the
L581@P24: production of a new expression. If a text is revised or modified, the resulting expression
L582@P24: is considered to be a new expression. Minor changes, such as corrections of spelling and
L583@P24: punctuation, etc., may be considered as variations within the same expression.
L584@P24: Examples
L585@P24: □ w1 Ellwanger’s Tennis--bis zum Turnierspieler
L586@P24: □ e1 the original German text
L587@P24: □ e2 the English translation by Wendy Gill
L588@P24: □ ….
L589@P24: □ w1 Franz Schubert’s Trout quintet
L590@P24: □ e1 the composer’s notated music
L591@P24: □ e2 the musical work as performed by Rosina Lhevinne, piano,
L592@P24: Stuart Sankey, double bass, and members of the Juilliard
L593@P24: String Quartet
L594@P24: □ e3 the musical work as performed by Jörg Demus, piano, and
L595@P24: the members of the Collegium Aureum
L596@P24: □ e4 the musical work as performed by Emanuel Ax, piano,
L597@P24: members of the Guarneri String Quartet, and Julius Levine,
L598@P24: double bass
L599@P24: □ ….
L600@P24: Defining expression as an entity in the model gives us a means of reflecting the
L601@P24: distinctions in intellectual or artistic content that may exist between one realization and
L602@P24: another of the same work. With expression defined as an entity, we can describe the
L603@P24: intellectual or artistic attributes of a particular realization of a work, and use the
L604@P24: differences in those attributes to signal differences in intellectual or artistic content.
L605@P24: Defining expression as an entity also enables us to draw relationships between specific
L606@P24: expressions of a work. We can use the entity called expression to identify, for example,
L607@P24: the specific text on which a translation is based, or the specific score used for the
L608@P24: performance of a musical composition.
L609@P24-25: 20 We can also use the entity defined as expression to indicate that the intellectual or artistic
L610@P25: content embodied in one manifestation is in fact the same, or substantially the same, as
L611@P25: that embodied in another manifestation. If two manifestations embody the same or almost
L612@P25: the same intellectual or artistic content, even though the physical embodiment may differ
L613@P25: and differing attributes of the manifestations may obscure the fact that the content is
L614@P25: similar in both, we can make the common link through the entity defined as expression.
L615@P25: On a practical level, the degree to which bibliographic distinctions are made between
L616@P25: variant expressions of a work will depend to some extent on the nature of the work itself,
L617@P25: and on the anticipated needs of users and on what the cataloguer can reasonably be
L618@P25: expected to recognize from the manifestation being described. Differences in form of
L619@P25: expression (e.g., the differences between the expression of a work in the form of
L620@P25: musical notation and the expression of the same work in the form of recorded sound) will
L621@P25: normally be reflected in the bibliographic record, no matter what the nature of the work

L606@P24: expressions of a work. We can use the entity called expression to identify, for example,
L607@P24: the specific text on which a translation is based, or the specific score used for the
L608@P24: performance of a musical composition.
L609@P24-25: 20 We can also use the entity defined as expression to indicate that the intellectual or artistic
L610@P25: content embodied in one manifestation is in fact the same, or substantially the same, as
L611@P25: that embodied in another manifestation. If two manifestations embody the same or almost
L612@P25: the same intellectual or artistic content, even though the physical embodiment may differ
L613@P25: and differing attributes of the manifestations may obscure the fact that the content is
L614@P25: similar in both, we can make the common link through the entity defined as expression.
L615@P25: On a practical level, the degree to which bibliographic distinctions are made between
L616@P25: variant expressions of a work will depend to some extent on the nature of the work itself,
L617@P25: and on the anticipated needs of users and on what the cataloguer can reasonably be
L618@P25: expected to recognize from the manifestation being described. Differences in form of
L619@P25: expression (e.g., the differences between the expression of a work in the form of
L620@P25: musical notation and the expression of the same work in the form of recorded sound) will
L621@P25: normally be reflected in the bibliographic record, no matter what the nature of the work
L622@P25: itself may be. Variant expressions in the same form (e.g., revised versions of a text) will
L623@P25: often be indirectly identified as different expressions because the variation is apparent
L624@P25: from the data associated with an attribute used to identify the manifestation in which the
L625@P25: expression is embodied (e.g., an edition statement). Variations that would be evident
L626@P25: only from a more detailed analysis and comparison of expressions (e.g., variations
L627@P25: between several of the early texts of Shakespeare's Hamlet) would normally be reflected
L628@P25: in the data only if the nature or stature of the work warranted such analysis, and only if it
L629@P25: was anticipated that the distinction would be important to users.
L630@P25: Variations within substantially the same expression (e.g., slight variations that can be
L631@P25: noticed between two states of the same edition in the case of hand press production)
L632@P25: would normally be ignored or, in specialized catalogues, be reflected as a note within the
L633@P25: bibliographic record for the manifestation. However, for some applications of the model
L634@P25: (e.g., early texts of rare manuscripts), each variation may be viewed as a different
L635@P25: expression.
L636@P25: 3.2.3 Manifestation
L637@P25: The third entity defined in the model is manifestation: the physical embodiment of an
L638@P25: expression of a work.
L639@P25: The entity defined as manifestation encompasses a wide range of materials, including
L640@P25: manuscripts, books, periodicals, maps, posters, sound recordings, films, video recordings,
L641@P25: CD-ROMs, multimedia kits, etc. As an entity, manifestation represents all the physical
L642@P25: objects that bear the same characteristics, in respect to both intellectual content and
L643@P25: physical form.
L644@P25: When a work is realized, the resulting expression of the work may be physically
L645@P25: embodied on or in a medium such as paper, audio tape, video tape, canvas, plaster, etc.
L646@P25: That physical embodiment constitutes a manifestation of the work. In some cases there
L647@P25: may be only a single physical exemplar produced of that manifestation of the work (e.g.,
L648@P25-26: 21 an author’s manuscript, a tape recorded for an oral history archive, an original oil
L649@P26: painting, etc.). In other cases there are multiple copies produced in order to facilitate
L650@P26: public dissemination or distribution. In those cases there is normally a more formal
L651@P26: production process involved, and a publisher, producer, or distributor takes responsibility
L652@P26: for the process. In other cases there may be only a limited number of copies made of an
L653@P26: original exemplar for purposes such as private study (e.g., a dubbing of an original
L654@P26: recording of a piece of music), or preservation (e.g., a photocopy produced on permanent
L655@P26: paper of an author’s original typescript). Whether the scope of production is broad (e.g.,
L656@P26: in the case of publication, etc.) or limited (e.g., in the case of copies made for private
L657@P26: study, etc.), the set of copies produced in each case constitutes a manifestation. All copies
L658@P26: produced that form part of the same set are considered to be copies of the same
L659@P26: manifestation.
L660@P26: The boundaries between one manifestation and another are drawn on the basis of both
L661@P26: intellectual content and physical form. When the production process involves changes in
L662@P26: physical form the resulting product is considered a new manifestation. Changes in
L663@P26: physical form include changes affecting display characteristics (e.g., a change in
L664@P26: typeface, size of font, page layout, etc.), changes in physical medium (e.g., a change from
L665@P26: paper to microfilm as the medium of conveyance), and changes in the container (e.g., a
L666@P26: change from cassette to cartridge as the container for a tape). Where the production
L667@P26: process involves a publisher, producer, distributor, etc., and there are changes signaled in
L668@P26: the product that are related to publication, marketing, etc. (e.g., a change in publisher,
L669@P26: repackaging, etc.), the resulting product may be considered a new manifestation.
L670@P26: Whenever the production process involves modifications, additions, deletions, etc. that
L671@P26: affect the intellectual or artistic content, the result is a new manifestation embodying a
L672@P26: new expression of the work.
L673@P26: Examples
L674@P26: □ w1 Harry Lindgren’s Geometric dissections
L675@P26: □ e1 original text entitled Geometric dissections
L676@P26: □ m1 the book published in 1964 by Van Nostrand
L677@P26: □ e2 revised text entitled Recreational problems in geometric

L704@P27: Changes that occur deliberately or even inadvertently in the production process that affect
L705@P27: the copies result, strictly speaking, in a new manifestation. A manifestation resulting
L706@P27: from such a change may be identified as a particular “state” or “issue” of the publication.
L707@P27: Changes that occur to an individual copy after the production process is complete (e.g.,
L708@P27: the loss of a page, rebinding, etc.) are not considered to result in a new manifestation.
L709@P27: That copy is simply considered to be an exemplar (or item) of the manifestation that
L710@P27: deviates from the copy as produced.
L711@P27: Defining manifestation as an entity enables us to name and describe the complete set of
L712@P27: items that result from a single act of physical embodiment or production. The entity
L713@P27: manifestation serves to describe the shared characteristics of copies of a particular
L714@P27: publication, edition, release, etc., as well as to describe unique productions such as
L715@P27: manuscripts, original oil paintings, etc.
L716@P27: With the entity defined as manifestation we can describe the physical characteristics of a
L717@P27: set of items and the characteristics associated with the production and distribution of that
L718@P27: set of items that may be important factors in enabling users to choose a manifestation
L719@P27-28: 23 appropriate to their physical needs and constraints, and to identify and acquire a copy of
L720@P28: that manifestation.
L721@P28: Defining manifestation as an entity also enables us to draw relationships between specific
L722@P28: manifestations of a work. We can use the relationships between manifestations to
L723@P28: identify, for example, the specific publication that was used to create a
L724@P28: microreproduction.
L725@P28: 3.2.4 Item
L726@P28: The fourth entity defined in the model is item: a single exemplar of a manifestation.
L727@P28: The entity defined as item is a concrete entity. It is in many instances a single physical
L728@P28: object (e.g., a copy of a one-volume monograph, a single audio cassette, etc.). There are
L729@P28: instances, however, where the entity defined as item comprises more than one physical
L730@P28: object (e.g., a monograph issued as two separately bound volumes, a recording issued on
L731@P28: three separate compact discs, etc.).
L732@P28: In terms of intellectual content and physical form, an item exemplifying a manifestation
L733@P28: is normally the same as the manifestation itself. However, variations may occur from one
L734@P28: item to another, even when the items exemplify the same manifestation, where those
L735@P28: variations are the result of actions external to the intent of the producer of the
L736@P28: manifestation (e.g., damage occurring after the item was produced, binding performed by
L737@P28: a library, etc.).
L738@P28: Examples
L739@P28: □ w1 Ronald Hayman’s Playback
L740@P28: □ e1 the author’s text edited for publication
L741@P28: □ m1 the book published in 1973 by Davis-Poynter
L742@P28: □ i1 copy autographed by the author
L743@P28: □ w1 Allan Wakeman’s Jabberwocky
L744@P28: □ e1 the author’s design for the game and text for the notes
L745@P28: □ m1 the game and accompanying notes for teachers
L746@P28: issued in 1974 by Longman
L747@P28: □ i1 copy lacking notes for teachers
L748@P28: Defining item as an entity enables us to separately identify individual copies of a
L749@P28: manifestation, and to describe those characteristics that are unique to that particular copy
L750@P28: and that pertain to transactions such as circulation, etc. involving that copy.
L751@P28-29: 24 Defining the entity called item also enables us to draw relationships between individual
L752@P29: copies of manifestations.
L753@P29: 3.2.5 Person
L754@P29: The fifth entity defined in the model is person: an individual.
L755@P29: The entity defined as person encompasses individuals that are deceased as well as those
L756@P29: that are living.
L757@P29: Examples
L758@P29: □ p1 Margaret Atwood
L759@P29: □ p2 Hans Christian Andersen
L760@P29: □ p3 Queen Victoria
L761@P29: □ p4 Anatole France
L762@P29: □ ….
L763@P29: For the purposes of this study persons are treated as entities only to the extent that they
L764@P29: are involved in the creation or realization of a work (e.g., as authors, composers, artists,
L765@P29: editors, translators, directors, performers, etc.), or are the subject of a work (e.g., as the
L766@P29: subject of a biographical or autobiographical work, of a history, etc.).
L767@P29: Defining the entity person enables us to name and identify the individual in a consistent
L768@P29: manner, independently of how the individual’s name appears on or in any particular
L769@P29: expression or manifestation of a work.
L770@P29: Defining person as an entity also enables us to draw relationships between a specific
L771@P29: person and a work or expression of a work for which that person may be responsible, or
L772@P29: between a work and the person that is the subject of the work.
L773@P29: 3.2.6 Corporate Body
L774@P29: The sixth entity defined in the model is corporate body: an organization or group of
L775@P29: individuals and/or organizations acting as a unit.
L776@P29: The entity defined as corporate body encompasses organizations and groups of
L777@P29: individuals and/or organizations that are identified by a particular name, including
L778@P29: occasional groups and groups that are constituted as meetings, conferences, congresses,
L779@P29: expeditions, exhibitions, festivals, fairs, etc. The entity also encompasses organizations
L780@P29: that act as territorial authorities, exercising or claiming to exercise government functions
L781@P29: over a certain territory, such as a federation, a state, a region, a local municipality, etc.
L782@P29-30: 25 The entity encompasses organizations and groups that are defunct as well as those that
L783@P30: continue to operate.
L784@P30: Examples
L785@P30: □ cb1 Museum of American Folk Art
L786@P30: □ cb2 BBC Symphony Orchestra
L787@P30: □ cb3 Symposium on Glaucoma
L788@P30: □ cb4 Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton
L789@P30: □ ….
L790@P30: For the purposes of this study corporate bodies are treated as entities only to the extent
L791@P30: that they are involved in the creation or realization of a work (e.g., as the sponsors or
L792@P30: endorsers of a work, etc.), or are the subject of a work (e.g., as the subject of a history,
L793@P30: etc.).
L794@P30: Defining the entity corporate body enables us to name and identify the organization or
L795@P30: group in a consistent manner, independently of how the name of the organization or
L796@P30: group appears on or in any particular expression or manifestation of a work.

L1436@P51: 4.5 Attributes of an Item
L1437@P51: The logical attributes of an item defined for this study are the following:
L1438@P51: item identifier
L1439@P51: fingerprint
L1440@P51: provenance of the item
L1441@P51: marks/inscriptions
L1442@P51: exhibition history
L1443@P51: condition of the item
L1444@P51: treatment history
L1445@P51: scheduled treatment
L1446@P51: access restrictions on the item
L1447@P51: Note: The attributes defined for the purposes of this study do not include those
L1448@P51: associated with transactions of an ephemeral nature such as the circulation or processing
L1449@P51: of an item.
L1450@P51: 4.5.1 Item Identifier
L1451@P51: The item identifier is a number or code that is uniquely associated with the item, and
L1452@P51: serves to differentiate that item from any other item in the same collection and/or
L1453@P51: institution (e.g., call number, accession number, bar code, etc.). The number is normally
L1454@P51: assigned by the institution that holds the item. The item identifier may also include a
L1455@P51: name or code identifying the institution or repository in which the item is housed, and a
L1456@P51-52: 47 name or code identifying a particular collection or sub-unit within the institution (e.g., a
L1457@P52: rare book collection, a branch library, etc.).
L1458@P52: 4.5.2 Fingerprint
L1459@P52: A fingerprint is an identifier constructed by combining groups of characters transcribed
L1460@P52: from specified pages of a printed item. The technique is used primarily to signal
L1461@P52: differences between individual copies of early printed books. There are various formulae
